channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: South Korea's economy grew 1.0% on the quarter in July to September, more than three times the 0.3% the Bank of Korea projected in August, with exports up 2.3% on semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment, according to preliminary data.
item.description:
Japan Today reports, citing preliminary Bank of Korea data, that South Korea's gross domestic product expanded 1.0% quarter on quarter in July to September, more than three times faster than the 0.3% growth the central bank projected in August. Exports increased 2.3%, driven by semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment, and real gross domestic income grew 18.8% on a year earlier, the fastest growth in almost 49 years. Handelsblatt reports that the International Monetary Fund raised its growth forecast for South Korea from 2.6% to 3.3% in mid-October, and that South Korea and Japan are Germany's most important export markets in Asia after China. The rows do not give the split of growth between consumption, investment and net exports, do not say what period the 2.3% export figure covers, and do not give the year-on-year GDP growth. They do not say whether the pace is expected to continue, and the data are preliminary.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a preliminary national figure, not company or product data. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, exports led by semiconductors point to strong electronics output in the region, and a preliminary figure can be revised. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, semiconductor and electronics manufacturing use specialty bonding, sealing and coating materials, so strong output could support demand for those materials in Asia, while the rows give no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the revision of the figure, the share of exports that goes to chip-related products, and the output data for electronics in the fourth quarter.

Japan Today | Handelsblatt

item.title: Moody's decided not to downgrade France's credit rating, and the French risk premium fell from 167 to 154 on Monday 26 October, its largest daily fall since 2020, according to Cinco Días.
item.description:
Cinco Días reports that Moody's decided not to downgrade France's credit rating. The decision followed a week in which the French risk premium had its largest weekly increase since 1990. After the announcement, the premium fell from 167 to 154 on Monday 26 October, a fall of 13 points and the largest daily fall since 2020. Moody's based its decision on its confidence that the government will approve a 2027 budget aimed at reducing the deficit, and in its main scenario it expects the government to approve the accounts by decree because of the fragmentation of parliament, a polarisation sharpened by the approach of the presidential elections. MarketScreener says French government bond prices rose on 26 October after Moody's spared France a downgrade, and that the selloff the week before had pushed the debt risk premium to its highest since the 2011 sovereign debt crisis. The Hürriyet Daily News says French bond yields reached their highest since 2002 last week, and that the ECB is expected to hold rates at its meeting on 29 October, with its focus likely to shift quickly to France according to Capital Economics' Andrew Kenningham. Cinco Días puts the rating at AA3, but the rows do not give the outlook, an exact date for the Moody's decision, the unit or benchmark of the premium, or the content of the budget.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a rating decision and a market reaction, not a change in the budget or in economic activity. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a lower risk premium eases financing costs for the French state and for companies, while a budget passed by decree can limit the political backing for the deficit plan. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, France is a large market for construction and manufacturing materials, and public spending and credit conditions influence construction activity, while the rows give no figures for the sector. Points that may be worth considering include the budget path, the ECB meeting on 29 October, and the French risk premium over the coming weeks.

Cinco Días | MarketScreener | Hürriyet Daily News

item.title: Iran, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye met in Tehran on 26 October and agreed to continue negotiations on regional security, described by the Pakistan Observer as the first direct high-level engagement between Iran and the other three.
item.description:
The Pakistan Observer reports that a four-party meeting hosted by Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, brought together representatives of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye with Iran. They agreed to continue negotiations on regional security and closer cooperation, keeping a diplomatic channel open while the war and rising tensions threaten stability across the region. The meeting focused on security challenges and opportunities for regional cooperation. The row says it was described as the first direct, high-level engagement during the current confrontation between Iran and the three countries, which the reports identify as members of the Makkah Joint Defence Pact. Middle East Monitor says the meeting began on 26 October and was to cover regional security, Israel's activities in the region, and developments in Palestine and Lebanon. The rows do not give any outcome beyond the agreement to continue talks, any commitment on shipping, a ceasefire or oil, the participation of the US or Israel, or a date for a next meeting. The Economic Times reports that oil edged lower on 27 October as diplomatic efforts raised hopes of a resolution, without naming this meeting.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe talks, not an agreement on the conflict. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, direct contact between Iran and Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye could lower the risk of escalation around shipping routes and energy sites, and a failure of talks could raise it, which would show in oil prices and freight and insurance costs. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, raw materials for resins and solvents depend on oil-based feedstocks, so changes in the risk premium could pass into raw-material prices with a delay, while the rows give no figures for chemicals. Points that may be worth considering include any statement after the meeting, the date of the next round, and the behaviour of oil and shipping rates.

Pakistan Observer | Middle East Monitor | The Economic Times

item.title: The Office of the US Trade Representative questions the status of the US–EU deal that paused duties on certain EU imports, after the European Investment Bank gave Airbus its largest loan ever and the USTR says it has no details of it.
item.description:
The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) said in a statement on 26 October that the status of the US–EU deal to pause duties on certain EU imports is in question after a record loan from the European Investment Bank (EIB) to Airbus. The USTR says France, Germany and Spain have supported Airbus to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and businesses. After the US won a WTO case and imposed significant duties on EU imports, it struck a deal with the EU to pause those duties in exchange for a mutual commitment to finance large civil aircraft producers on market terms. This summer, almost immediately after the EU extended the pause, the EIB awarded Airbus its largest loan ever for projects in France, Germany and Spain. The USTR says that, despite repeated requests, it still has no details of the loan, that this injects substantial uncertainty into transatlantic trade in aerospace, and that it is important to resolve it as soon as possible to avoid a violation of the deal. The statement is the US account. It does not give the size or terms of the loan, the EU's or Airbus's response, a deadline, a decision to reinstate duties, or the duty rates and products covered.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The statement raises a question about a pause and does not reinstate any duty. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, if the paused duties returned, they would raise the cost of the covered EU goods in the US and could prompt a response from the EU, which would add to the existing trade tensions. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, aircraft structures, interiors and engines use specialty bonding, sealing and coating materials, so a dispute that affects aircraft production or trade could change demand for those materials, while the statement gives no product list. Points that may be worth considering include the EU's and Airbus's response, the products covered by the paused duties, and any date set by the USTR.

Office of the United States Trade Representative
item.source: Office of the United States Trade Representative

item.title: Bloomberg reports, citing informed sources, that the EU may publish safeguard measures in the form of import caps or tariffs on Chinese chemicals, furniture and machinery as early as the first quarter of 2027.
item.description:
Lianhe Zaobao reports, citing Bloomberg and informed sources, that the European Union may publish some safeguard measures as early as the first quarter of next year to reduce imports of Chinese chemicals, furniture and machinery products, in the form of import caps or tariffs. Cnyes says the EU intends to propose a new wave of import defence measures as early as the first quarter of 2027, and Commercial Times states without attribution that more import restrictions will be imposed in that quarter. According to Zaobao, the European Commission is trying to balance support for European industry against the risk of retaliation by China that could lead to a trade war. Cnyes adds that the EU and China recently agreed to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 units a year, which the EU believes will reduce the likelihood of retaliation. The Zaobao and Cnyes reports rest on unnamed sources and the words "may" or "intends to propose" with "as early as". They do not give a product list or customs codes, the size of any cap or the level of any tariff, the legal instrument, a statement by the Commission, or which member states support the plan.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a possible plan, not a decision. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a safeguard measure is a temporary limit on imports of a product when a surge in imports harms producers in the importing region, and caps or tariffs on chemicals would change the supply and price of those chemicals in Europe, with retaliation by China possible. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, chemicals include raw materials for bonding, sealing and coating materials, and furniture manufacturing uses adhesives to bond panels, foam and fabrics, so measures on those products could change raw-material costs, supplier choice and the volume of furniture made in Europe, while the rows give no products. Points that may be worth considering include the Commission's formal proposal and product list, the timing in the first quarter, and China's response.

Lianhe Zaobao | Cnyes | Commercial Times

item.title: UK annual house price inflation eased from 1.2% in July to 0.9% in August, with the Office for National Statistics citing a 5.0% fall in flat prices over 12 months as a factor in a 2.2% fall in London property values.
item.description:
The Independent, citing the Office for National Statistics (ONS), reports that the average annual rate of house price inflation in the UK eased from 1.2% in July to 0.9% in August, and its headline calls it the fourth consecutive monthly slowdown. The ONS cited a 5.0% fall in flat prices over the 12 months as a factor in a 2.2% fall in average property values in London in the year to August. The ONS also reports that the average monthly private rent in the UK was GBP 1,406 in September 2026, 3.8% more than a year earlier. The row mixes a house price series that ends in August and a rent series that ends in September, so the two are not compared. It does not give the average UK house price, figures for regions other than London, transaction volumes, mortgage rates, or the prices of houses as against flats.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports price indices, not construction output or renovation spending. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, slower price growth and falling flat prices can weaken the case for new residential projects and for owners to invest in their homes, while rising rents can support demand for rental housing. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, housing construction and renovation are applications for bonding, sealing and coating materials, so a softer housing market could weigh on demand for those materials in the UK, while the row gives no volumes. Points that may be worth considering include UK housing starts and completions, the effect of mortgage rates on transactions, and whether the slowdown spreads from flats to houses.

The Independent

item.title: The Center of Automotive Management finds that ten of the world's 15 leading automotive groups recorded declining sales by the end of September, with BMW, Mercedes and Volkswagen suffering particularly severe losses and cutting even more jobs.
item.description:
The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports an analysis by the Center of Automotive Management (CAM), based in Bergisch Gladbach, of the world's 15 leading automotive groups. Ten of them recorded declining sales figures by the end of September this year. BMW, Mercedes and Volkswagen are suffering particularly severe losses compared with the rest of the industry, and the three German groups are cutting even more jobs. At Volkswagen alone, up to 100,000 jobs worldwide are expected to be lost in the coming years. This is one source. The row does not give the comparison period, such as the same months of the previous year, or the size of the falls, and it does not say whether "sales figures" means vehicles sold or revenue. It does not name the five groups whose sales rose, give the number of jobs at BMW and Mercedes, or give a timetable for the job cuts.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a count of groups with falling sales, not the size of the fall or production volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, falling sales and job cuts at large producers point to lower output plans, which feed through to suppliers with a delay. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, cars use bonding, sealing and coating materials in the body, glass, interior and battery, so lower vehicle volumes could reduce demand for those materials, while a shift of the mix towards electric models could change the amount used per vehicle, and the row gives no figures for either. Points that may be worth considering include the comparison period and the volumes behind the analysis, the production plans of the three German groups, and the groups whose sales rose.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: US Central Command says it helped Gulf states export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via the Strait of Hormuz since the summer and that over 3,000 ships passed with its support; the US Secretary of State says exports are at pre-conflict level.
item.description:
The Hong Kong Economic Times reports that US Central Command said on 25 October it has helped Gulf states bypass Iran's blockade and export 1.5 billion barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz since the summer, and that over 3,000 merchant ships passed with its support. Its commander, Admiral Brad Cooper, said the main transit route is now free of Iranian mines. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said oil exports through the strait are at the same level as before the US–Iran conflict began, that the strait remains open and that Iran has lost control of it. Al Jazeera gives the ship count for the past six months, not since the summer, and says more than 95% of ships that navigated the channel in recent months passed safely despite Iranian threats. It adds that Kpler, a market data firm, put oil leaving the Gulf region excluding Iran at least 16.5 million barrels a day in September, equal to the pre-war average, while oil prices remain far above pre-war levels. MarketScreener reports that Singapore's energy and trade minister, Tan See Leng, warned about the impact of the "continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz" and of escalation after Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure. The rows do not reconcile an open strait with a "continued closure", and they give no independent flow data for October, no refined-product flows, no insurance or freight terms, and no number of ships that passed without escort.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a military count and official statements, not independent measurements of flows. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a route that is open but depends on naval support can carry crude and products while still adding insurance and freight costs, and the oil price reflects perceived risk as well as volumes. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, many resins, polymers and solvents are priced off crude oil and its derivatives, so continued flows could limit supply gaps while a risk premium could stay in raw-material prices, while the rows give no figures for chemicals. Points that may be worth considering include independent shipping and Kpler data for October, refined-product flows out of the Gulf, insurance and freight rates through the strait, and any change in the escort arrangement.

Hong Kong Economic Times | Al Jazeera | MarketScreener

item.title: Brazil's real fell by more than 10% against the dollar in early trading on 26 October, and the Ibovespa fell more than 10% at the open, which briefly halted trading, after President Lula's re-election in the runoff of 25 October.
item.description:
The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports that the Bovespa index of the São Paulo Stock Exchange fell more than 10% at the start of trading on 26 October, triggering a trading halt, and that the real fell by 11% against the dollar. It says the iShares MSCI Brazil fund, traded in New York, was down by more than 25% before the main session, and that J.P. Morgan lowered its rating of the real while Bradesco BBI cut its outlook for Brazilian stocks to "Neutral". Der Standard says the exchange operator B3 interrupted trading automatically for 30 minutes. The Financial Times calls it the worst single-day market rout in decades and says investors were warning about the state of public finances, with some domestic bond yields above 15%. MarketScreener, citing LSEG data, gives a low for the Ibovespa 17% down and says the dollar rose over 12%, while the Financial Times gives 15% for equities and almost 12% for the real, and the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung 11% for the real, so the rows differ on the depth. MarketScreener adds that Telefónica fell 7.2%, Santander close to 4% and AB InBev 3.5% in early trade, and La Nacion says Chicago soybean prices fell USD 8.45 a tonne, linked to the US crop and the real. The rows do not give closing levels or any central bank action.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report price moves in the first session after the result, not closing levels or a change in policy. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a weaker currency raises the local-currency cost of imported inputs and equipment for Brazilian producers while lifting the value of dollar earnings for exporters, and higher bond yields raise borrowing costs for construction and manufacturing. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Brazil is a market for construction and industrial materials, so a currency fall and higher rates could change import costs, pricing and project financing, while the rows give no figures for the sector. Points that may be worth considering include the closing levels and any central bank response, the budget plans of the new government, and the real against the dollar in the coming sessions.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Der Standard | The Financial Times | MarketScreener | MarketScreener | La Nacion

item.title: The German government has presented a draft law on a voluntary "Building Type E" standard that would let contract parties agree to waive certain comfort standards, and Handelsblatt says costs can be cut by 10 to 15%, according to pilot projects.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that the federal government has presented a draft law for simpler and cheaper construction, given the housing shortage. By amending construction contract law, builders could build faster by waiving certain comfort standards, according to a draft from the Ministry of Justice on the "Building Type E". Construction costs can be reduced by ten to 15%, according to experience from pilot projects. The regulation is voluntary: the simplified rules apply only if the parties expressly agree to the "Building Type E basic standard", and otherwise the previous, higher standards remain in force. Handelsblatt and WirtschaftsWoche, in reports before the presentation, name Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig and Construction Minister Verena Hubertz, both SPD, as presenting the bill. Hubig says that building must become easier and cheaper to create more housing, and Handelsblatt describes the solution as doing without expensive extras that have become common but are not mandatory. The rows do not say which standards can be waived, give the legislative timetable or the need for approval by the Bundestag and Bundesrat, or describe how many pilot projects the cost figure rests on.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a draft law and a contract option, not a change in the building rules or in product requirements. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, waiving standards by agreement works through the specification of what is built, and savings of 10 to 15% could come from simpler fittings and fewer extras, so the effect on materials demand depends on which standards are waived. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, standards for matters such as sound insulation, moisture protection or flooring can set the use of bonding, sealing and coating materials in building construction, so waiving some of them could reduce demand for certain products, while a faster and cheaper build-out could support volumes, and the rows do not say which standards are covered. Points that may be worth considering include the text of the draft and the standards it names, the timetable in the Bundestag and Bundesrat, and the results of the pilot projects.

Handelsblatt | Handelsblatt | WirtschaftsWoche

item.title: Chinese-branded cars made up 12.7% of European car registrations in the third quarter of 2026, ahead of Japanese brands at 11.9%, the first time over a full quarter, according to the market researcher Dataforce.
item.description:
The Straits Times, citing Dataforce, reports that Chinese-branded car registrations in Europe made up 12.7% of total sales in the third quarter of 2026, outselling Japanese brands for the first time over a full quarter. Japanese manufacturers, including Toyota, accounted for 11.9%. The Los Angeles Times adds that registrations of Chinese-branded cars roughly doubled from a year earlier in the three months through September, led by hybrids, and that the advance accelerated at the end of the quarter: in September the Chinese brands' share reached a record 14.5%, almost three percentage points above August. The rows do not define which countries make up "Europe", do not give registration volumes or the year-earlier shares, do not say how many of the cars are built in China and how many in Europe, and do not name the brands or give the split by drive type beyond hybrids leading the growth. They also do not say whether the Japanese share fell or whether total registrations grew.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report shares of registrations, not volumes or the origin of the components. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a shift in share changes which manufacturers and supplier networks specify materials, not how many cars are needed in total, and models of Chinese brands may use different suppliers from European or Japanese models. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, car bodies, battery packs, glass and interiors are bonded, sealed and coated during assembly, so a shift of volume towards Chinese-brand models could change which suppliers are qualified, while the rows give no supplier data. Points that may be worth considering include Chinese-brand registrations in volumes, the share built in Europe against imported, and the effect of EU trade defence measures on that share.

The Straits Times | Los Angeles Times
